text.text: We are claiming that scaling current architectures on current objectives is not, by itself, a demonstrated path to autonoetic self-consciousness.
Fourth, many of the framework's current predictions are null predictions, and this is a real limitation.

Most of the protocols described above predict that present systems will fail, with no value dimension that survives decoupling, ownership at chance, no internal source classification in the direct-answer condition, and no goal revision that traces to anything but task conditions or an objective term.
Several protocols cannot be administered to text-only models at all, and the protocols address only the past-directed part of autonoetic consciousness.

Episodic future projection, which Tulving's definition includes and which Layer 3's constructive machinery would serve, has no protocol in this set, and neither does retrieval gating, the other autonoetic component of Layer 4.
Predicting absence is weaker than predicting a positive signature, because many architectures could produce a null result for reasons unrelated to AAM.
The positive predictions, what a system instantiating all five layers should exhibit, are specified but not yet observed, since no such system currently exists.
For that reason, the prescriptive column of Figure 2 is a design target rather than an empirical result.

text.text: This asymmetry is unavoidable when an architectural proposal precedes the construction of systems designed to satisfy it.
It is partly mitigated in two ways.
First, several protocols predict dissociations rather than flat failures.

For example, success at locating supporting passages combined with failure at internal source monitoring would be a positive, falsifiable pattern, and its persistence with scale is what separates AAM from a scalar account.
Second, human developmental dissociations give the positive predictions independent empirical content, because they show that the proposed layer combinations occur in real cognitive systems.
Still, until an AAM-targeted system exists, the strongest empirical claims AAM can make about current artificial systems are claims about what they lack.
The criterion AAM cares about is architectural, whereas the protocols are behavioral, so a sufficiently capable simulator could in principle pass an individual protocol.

That caveat applies to the inference from the protocols to the target capacity, for which they are defeasible, converging indicators, and not to the dependency claim, which one controlled counterexample refutes.
What marks instantiation is the joint dissociation pattern across protocols, which the underlying architecture explains more parsimoniously than protocol-byprotocol mimicry.
Four further objections deserve naming.

First, evolution fixed core interoceptive setpoints, such as those for glucose and temperature, so the ontogenetic claim in Layer 1 cannot be that every value dimension is constructed within a lifetime.
The narrower claim is that the set of dimensions is open and new ones can be constructed from the organism's regulatory history, whereas an objective function closes the set.
Construction runs through the inherited setpoints, since a variable that has predicted violation of one comes to be regulated.
AAM takes the mark of a constructed dimension to be that regulation persists after the predictive link closes, which is what the decoupling arm of Protocol 1 measures.
A learned predictor of an old dimension, in an animal or a reinforcementlearning agent, extinguishes with the link.
Second, reinforcement learning from human feedback is an environment a system learns from, and the distinction drawn in Layer 3 between an environment and a specification might seem to admit it.
It does not, because the reward model specifies the value axes and the environment supplies data about them.
Third, the adequacy constraint assumes that the five human roles are the right decomposition.

That is a hypothesis, defeasible by a system that achieves autonoetic self-consciousness under a different decomposition, and the framework's claim is only that any such system must explain how it realizes the roles the human case distributes across these layers.
Fourth, treating uncontrolled passes as heuristics could make positive results non-confirmatory by construction.

The adjudication rule above closes that route, because a controlled pass is confirmatory and a controlled pass at a component of a higher layer while a layer it depends on is absent is disconfirmatory.
The debate over machine consciousness has often been framed as a problem for philosophy and computer science.
It is also a problem for cognitive psychology, which has spent decades characterizing how self-aware cognition is assembled in human development.
The Autobiographical Architecture Model applies developmental evidence to artificial systems.

Its central claim is that current AI systems lack the architecture of an autonoetic self, and that, on the evidence to date, the gaps at Layers 1 and 3 are architectural rather than merely scalar, while the gap at Layer 4's source monitoring is one of training objective and readout.
AAM does not claim that artificial systems must recapitulate human development, nor that human development provides the only possible route to autonoetic self-consciousness.

What it provides is a candidate template, derived from the best-characterized case we have, against which artificial systems can be evaluated (see the benchmark protocols and Figure 2), and its predictions are empirically tractable in ways they were not a few years ago.

text.text: The framework supplements indicator-property approaches with a developmental and architectural dimension.
It asks whether the markers of self-awareness a system displays are integrated in the right way.
The practical implication is that narrative fluency should not be mistaken for autonoetic selfhood.

The theoretical implication is that assessments of machine consciousness need to move beyond lists of capacities toward models of how those capacities are developmentally and architecturally organized.
The central question is whether an artificial system has an architecture capable of remembering, monitoring, and revising a self across time, not whether it can describe one.
Can closed-loop allostatic regulation be implemented in non-biological substrates?
Layer 1 requires value dimensions that can expand in response to self-generated viability constraints, which adaptive control and reward reweighting do not supply.

Comparative work on open-ended value construction in animals, and research on soft robotics and homeostatic machines (Man & Damasio, 2019), are relevant but remain underused in debates about AI consciousness.
